But founders should not confuse one exceptional company with a full market reset. The lesson is to separate the existence of winners from the claim that the whole sector has returned to easy mode.

trace.answer:
So you know we've been talking for years about what's happening with AI in B2B software.
And so many folks have told me they're just waiting for their opportunity.
Well I think there is one now.
The market cap on public SaaS companies is down 30%.
We got our first real data this week from Adobe Sign / EchoSign which showed that sign ups were way down after ChatGPT launched.
But here's where things get interesting:
SaaStr Annual was March 10-12,
and when everyone came together, I asked them all what they thought would happen with AI and SaaS in the next year.
I'm going to share with you some of the most interesting answers.
One thing that was clear to almost everyone at the event was that while overall sales and marketing spend was under pressure across the board right now—many leaders still had budget to invest in AI.
In fact, according to Bessemer Venture Partners' latest report, enterprise spending on AI infrastructure alone will reach an estimated $140 billion by 2029.
But here's the catch—and why I think this presents a huge opportunity if you can tap into it—the same report found that roughly two-thirds of enterprises lack dedicated IT resources to implement these new tools.
Translation? There's massive demand, but nobody knows how to actually deploy it yet.
This creates a perfect storm for founders like us who want to build in B2B + AI. The market needs solutions badly, but the traditional players haven't figured out how to deliver them yet. Now let me give you a quick update on where I see markets headed. We'll start with Figma. Figma just hit $304 million in a single quarter growing 40%, crossing $1 Billion ARR. So far, no slowdown. And then also, Atlassian, Snowflake, MongoDB, Asana, Zoominfo, Salesforce, Slack and more all put up strong numbers too.
Figma grew 40% year-over-year, hitting $300 million quarterly, and crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate.
They added 17,000 net new users, bringing total DAUs to 25 million.
Forbes 2000 adoption jumped 38% year over year, reaching 82% penetration among Fortune 500 companies.
Their non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 21% in fiscal '25, exceeding guidance.
But perhaps most importantly, their average revenue per employee rose 39% year-over-year, driven by efficient expansion and better unit economics.
With 77% of revenue coming from outside the US and nearly half generated internationally, Figma continues to prove that product-led growth works globally regardless of borders. They ended FY25 with approximately $1.5 billion in cash and zero debt. But here's where it gets really interesting. Their non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 21% in fiscal '25, exceeding guidance.
Average revenue per employee rose 39% year-over-year, driven by efficient expansion and better unit economics.
The company remains highly profitable, with 19% adjusted operating margins in Q4 and 15% adjusted operating margins in full fiscal 2025.
These aren't the margins you'd expect from a growth-stage company.
They're the kind of margins you'd typically associate with mature SaaS businesses approaching IPO scale. Why This Matters For Founders
Let me break down exactly why these numbers matter for anyone building in B2B today.
